description.short: Lighter and more aromatic than the second flush — fresh, brisk black tea from broad-leaf Assam bushes
description.overview: Assam is the world's largest tea-growing region by production volume, situated in the plains along the Brahmaputra River under hot, humid conditions ideal for the large-leaf var. assamica cultivar.
description.leaf: Large, twisted, dark brown leaf with golden tips
description.aroma: Fresh, malty, with subtle floral notes characteristic of the first flush
description.taste: Brisk, malty, slightly lighter in body and astringency than the second flush
description.processing: Plucking → withering → rolling (CTC or orthodox method) → full oxidation → drying

history.origin: Tea bushes in Assam were discovered by the British in 1823 by Scottish adventurer Robert Bruce through the local Singpho tribe, who had long consumed wild tea.
history.development: The British East India Company initiated commercial tea cultivation in Assam during the 1830s–1840s, laying the foundation for the entire Indian tea industry.
history.modern: Today, Assam is the world's largest tea-producing region by volume, supplying a major portion of global black tea, including most commercial breakfast blends.
interestingFacts: Assam is the only region in the world where the large-leaf Camellia sinensis var. assamica grows natively in the wild, which later gave the botanical variety its name.
The discovery of indigenous tea plants in Assam ended China's monopoly on tea and established India as China's primary rival in the global market.
